1.note: Moses is using the term **brothers** to describe people who are descended from the same ancestor. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your fellow Israelite]

The expression **be scattered** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [wandering away]

Here Moses is speaking as if a person could literally **hide yourself from them** when seeing lost animals. This is a metaphor for deliberately ignoring something that needs attention and avoiding responsibility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. This same phrasing appears in verses 3–4 as well. Alternate translation: [pretend you do not see them] or [deliberately ignore your responsibility to help]

The word **yourself** indicates that the object of the verb is the same as the subject of the verb. Moses is emphasizing that a person should not deliberately avoid helping when they see a lost animal. Use a way that is natural in your language to indicate that the same person fills two roles in the sentence. Alternate translation: [pretend not to see them] or [deliberately ignore them]

Moses is repeating forms of the verb **return** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. This emphasizes the obligation to definitely return the lost animal. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [you must certainly return them] or [you absolutely must return them]

2.q: וְ⁠אִם־לֹ֨א קָר֥וֹב אָחִ֛י⁠ךָ אֵלֶ֖י⁠ךָ וְ⁠לֹ֣א יְדַעְתּ֑⁠וֹ וַ⁠אֲסַפְתּ⁠וֹ֙
2.note: Moses is describing a possible condition in which someone would only take the lost animal to his home if the owner either lives far away or is unknown to the finder. Express this possible condition in a way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And if you do not know who owns the animal or the owner lives far away from you, then bring it home]

3.q: וְ⁠כֵ֧ן תַּעֲשֶׂ֣ה לַ⁠חֲמֹר֗⁠וֹ וְ⁠כֵ֣ן תַּעֲשֶׂה֮ לְ⁠שִׂמְלָת⁠וֹ֒ וְ⁠כֵ֣ן תַּעֲשֶׂ֜ה לְ⁠כָל־אֲבֵדַ֥ת אָחִ֛י⁠ךָ אֲשֶׁר־תֹּאבַ֥ד מִמֶּ֖⁠נּוּ וּ⁠מְצָאתָ֑⁠הּ
3.note: Moses uses a repetitive series of clauses to communicate that what he is saying should be understood as comprehensive. He repeats “and thus you shall do” for different items to emphasize that this principle applies to all lost possessions, not just livestock. Use a form in your language that someone would use to describe a situation that is comprehensive. Alternate translation: [Do the same for his donkey, his clothing, and anything else your fellow Israelite loses that you find]

4.note: Moses is repeating forms of the verb **lift** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. This emphasizes the obligation to definitely help the fallen animal. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [you must certainly help it up] or [you absolutely must assist in getting it back on its feet]

5.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **abomination**, you could express the same idea in another way. The term refers to something that disgusts or deeply offends Yahweh. Alternate translation: [are detestable] or [are greatly offensive]
See how you translated the phrase “Yahweh your God” in 1:10. Alternate translation: [to Yahweh, the God we worship]

6.note: Here, **to your face** represents being in front of something. Moses is using this expression to describe something an Israelite might encounter directly in their path. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in front of you] or [along your way]

7.note: Moses is repeating forms of the verb **send** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. This emphasizes the absolute requirement to release the mother bird. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [You must certainly let the mother bird go free] or [You absolutely must release the mother bird]

Here, **so that** marks **it may go well with you, and you may prolong your days** as the goal or purpose of following the command to release the mother bird. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [for if you do this, then things will go well for you and you will have a long life] or [by doing this, you will ensure prosperity and a long life]
See how you translated the phrase “prolong your days” in 4:26. Alternate translation: [and you may live for many years] or [and you may have a long life]

8.note: A **railing** is a kind of protective barrier or wall built around the edge of a flat roof to prevent people from falling off. In ancient Israel, roofs were typically flat and used as living spaces, making safety features necessary. If your readers would not be familiar with what a railing is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [a protective fence around the edge of your flat roof] or [a safety barrier surrounding the perimeter of your rooftop]

Here, **and** marks **you will not bring blood on your house** as the goal or purpose of making a railing for the roof. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [so that you will not be responsible for the death] or [in this way, you will prevent becoming liable for someone’s death]

Here, **blood** represents guilt for someone’s death. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in order to avoid being guilty of causing someone’s death]

Moses is describing a possible condition in which homeowners would be responsible for bloodguilt only if someone falls from their roof without a railing. Express this possible condition in a way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [should anyone ever fall from your roof and die] or [in case someone were to fall from your roof and die]

9.note: Planting a vineyard with two kinds of seed was a symbolic action that showed the importance of maintaining separation and purity. This prohibition represented how Israel was to remain distinct and set apart from other nations, not mixing their religious and cultural practices with those of surrounding peoples. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [You shall not mix different types of seed in your vineyard to show that you must remain pure and unmixed with other nations]

9.q: פֶּן־תִּקְדַּ֗שׁ הַֽ⁠מְלֵאָ֤ה הַ⁠זֶּ֨רַע֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר תִּזְרָ֔ע וּ⁠תְבוּאַ֖ת הַ⁠כָּֽרֶם
9.note: Moses is using the word translated as **lest** to introduce an outcome that he does not want to happen. Because of this, he first gives the Israelites an instruction to follow so that this will not happen. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that avoiding this outcome is the purpose of the instruction. Alternate translation: [otherwise all the produce of the seed that you have sown and the yield of the vineyard will be set apart]

This could mean: (1) the crops would become dedicated to Yahweh, and sent to the priests and Levites for their food. Alternate translation: [be dedicated to Yahweh] or (2) the crops would be defiled and could not be eaten by anyone or offered to Yahweh. Alternate translation: [be defiled and have to be destroyed]

11.note: The term **wool** is a kind of soft, curly fiber that grows on sheep, and **linen** is a kind of fabric made from flax plant fibers. If your readers would not be familiar with what wool and linen are, you could use the names of similar materials that your readers would recognize, or you could use more general terms. Alternate translation: [animal fiber and plant fiber] or [sheep hair fabric and flax plant fabric]

12.note: The term **tassels** is used for a kind of decorative bunch of threads or cords that are tied together at one end and hang freely at the other end. These were attached to the corners of garments for religious purposes to help Israelites remember God’s commandments. If your readers would not be familiar with what a tassel is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [decorative thread bundles] or [hanging cord ornaments]

13.note: Moses is referring to sexual relations in a polite way by using the phrase **he goes in to her**. Depending on what is helpful in your language, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [and he consummates the marriage with her] or [and he has sexual relations with her]

Moses is introducing a possible condition that he describes in this verse and the next. The instruction for what the parents should do if this condition happens comes in verse 15. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a situation such as this.

14.note: Moses is referring to sexual immorality in a polite way by using the phrase **accuses her of shameful things**. This refers to a husband claiming his wife was not a virgin before marriage. Depending on what is helpful in your language, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [and accuses her of immoral behavior before marriage] or [and claims she was sexually active before they married]

Here, **name** represents “reputation.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and damages her reputation] or [and spreads rumors that harm how others view her]

14.q: וְ⁠אָמַ֗ר אֶת־הָ⁠אִשָּׁ֤ה הַ⁠זֹּאת֙ לָקַ֔חְתִּי וָ⁠אֶקְרַ֣ב אֵלֶ֔י⁠הָ וְ⁠לֹא־מָצָ֥אתִי לָ֖⁠הּ בְּתוּלִֽים
14.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [and publicly declares that he took this woman and came near to her but did not find her virginity]

The husband is referring to sexual relations in a polite way by using the phrase **I came near to her**. Depending on what is helpful in your language, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [and I was intimate with her] or [and I had sexual relations with her]

15.note: Here, **virginity of the girl** represents physical evidence of the girl’s virginity, which would typically be a cloth with bloodstains from the wedding night. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [evidence of the girl’s virginity] or [the bloodstained cloth that proves the girl was a virgin]

16.q: וְ⁠אָמַ֛ר אֲבִ֥י הַֽנַּעֲרָ֖ה אֶל־הַ⁠זְּקֵנִ֑ים אֶת־בִּתִּ֗⁠י נָתַ֜תִּי לָ⁠אִ֥ישׁ הַ⁠זֶּ֛ה לְ⁠אִשָּׁ֖ה וַ⁠יִּשְׂנָאֶֽ⁠הָ׃ וְ⁠הִנֵּה־ה֡וּא שָׂם֩ עֲלִילֹ֨ת דְּבָרִ֜ים לֵ⁠אמֹ֗ר לֹֽא־מָצָ֤אתִי לְ⁠בִתְּ⁠ךָ֙ בְּתוּלִ֔ים וְ⁠אֵ֖לֶּה בְּתוּלֵ֣י בִתִּ֑⁠י
16.note: There are three levels of quotation here. Moses is speaking (level 1) and quoting the father of the bride (level 2) explaining what the groom said (level 3). Use the appropriate punctuation in your language to mark these levels of quotation. Alternatively, you could translate this so that there is not a third-level quotation.

17.note: See how you translated the phrase “shameful things” in verse 14 and the term “virginity” in verse 15.

Moses is using the expression **to the faces of** to mean “before” or “in the presence of” the elders. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [before] or [to show]

19.q: וְ⁠עָנְשׁ֨וּ אֹת֜⁠וֹ & כִּ֤י הוֹצִיא֙ שֵׁ֣ם רָ֔ע עַ֖ל בְּתוּלַ֣ת יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל
19.note: The word **because** introduces the reason for the punishment that is described. If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases and combine them at the beginning of the verse, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [and for bringing a bad name upon a virgin of Israel, they shall fine him]

**100 silvers** refers to a common monetary unit for Israelites. You could try to express this in terms of modern money values, but if you did, that could cause your Bible translation to become outdated and inaccurate, since those values can change over time. Instead, you might say something general like “100 silver coins,” or “100 pieces of silver,” or use the biblical term in the text and explain the value in a note.
See how you translated the expression “a bad name” in 22:14.

20.note: Moses uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between the previous case (where the accusation against the girl was false) and this case (where the accusation might be true). In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [However, if this accusation is true]

Moses is describing a possible situation in which certain consequences will follow only if the accusation against the young woman is true. The description of the possible situation begins in verse 13 and the consequences are described in verse 21. Express this possible condition in a way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [But should this accusation prove true]

The expression **was not found** contains a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that the man did not find proof that the girl was a virgin]
See how you translated this similar situation in 22:14–15. Alternate translation: [evidence was not found proving that the young woman had kept herself pure until marriage]

21.note: See how you translated this same phrase in 13:5.

22.note: The expression **is found** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [If someone finds a man]

Moses is referring to sexual intercourse in a polite way by using the phrase **lying with**. Depending on what is helpful in your language, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [having intimate relations with] or [having sex with]
See how you translated this similar phrase in the previous verse.

23.note: Moses is introducing a possible situation in this verse and in the next verse he gives the instructions for what to do if this situation occurs. Express this possible condition in a way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [If it should happen that a virgin girl who is]

Moses is referring to sexual intercourse in a polite way by using the phrase **lies with her**. Depending on what is helpful in your language, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [and is intimate with her] or [and has sexual relations with her]

24.note: Moses is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [because she did not cry out for help when she was attacked]
The word **you** is plural here. So use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Although the woman was only engaged, not yet married, she was called a “wife” because in Israelite culture, an engaged woman was legally considered to belong to her future husband. Some cultures might need to explain this concept in a footnote.
See how you translated this same phrase in 13:5.

26.note: Moses is using **sin of death** as a common expression of his culture to mean “an offense deserving the death penalty.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [offense deserving death] or [crime worthy of execution]

26.q: כִּ֡י כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁר֩ יָק֨וּם אִ֤ישׁ עַל־רֵעֵ֨⁠הוּ֙ וּ⁠רְצָח֣⁠וֹ נֶ֔פֶשׁ כֵּ֖ן הַ⁠דָּבָ֥ר הַ⁠זֶּֽה
26.note: This is referring to the situation described in [21:1](ta:21) and following.

28.note: The expression **are discovered** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [if somebody finds out what happened]

29.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 22:19.

Moses is referring to sexual assault by using the phrase **violated her**. Depending on what is helpful in your language, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [he dishonored her] or [he forced her to have sexual relations]

30.note: Moses is referring to sexual relations with a father’s wife in a polite way by using the phrase **take the wife of his father**. Depending on what is helpful in your language, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [shall not marry his father’s wife] or [shall not have sexual relations with his father’s wife]

Moses is using **uncover the hem of his father** as a common expression of his culture to mean “dishonor his father.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he shall not dishonor his father’s marriage bed]
